title: GPX Timestamp Remover: Strip the <time> Tags
description: Remove time elements from a GPX file with the GPX Timestamp Remover — geometry preserved, clock gone, processed locally. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, stripping <time> from a typical trackpoint shrinks it from 97 to 64 bytes — a third of every point — and the track becomes a pure shape that says where, never when.
quick_answer: The GPX Timestamp Remover strips the <time> elements from a GPX file and downloads a geometry-preserving copy without them. Load the file locally, remove the clock, and share the route as pure geography — useful when the path is public information but your schedule is not.
steps_intro: The route stays; the timetable goes:

body.t: Timestamps reveal when you were where — home departure times included. A timeless copy shares the trail without the diary. Strip altitude the same way with the
A published route is a plan, not a recording. Removing times stops readers mistaking your Tuesday for the route's property.
A device with a dead clock stamped everything 2015. If the times cannot be repaired (the
handles honest offsets), an untimed file beats a lying one.
Some minimal consumers expect pure geometry; the stripped copy is the compatible edition, with speed expectations removed along with the stamps.

examples.label: Example · One point, before and after

body.t: Before: <trkpt lat="40.768100" lon="-73.971900"><ele>102.4</ele><time>2026-10-04T07:00:00Z</time></trkpt> — 97 bytes. After: 64 bytes, same coordinates, same elevation, no clock. The shape of the day survives; its schedule does not.

Speed, pace, duration and every time-based statistic go silent on a timeless file — there is nothing to divide distance by. That silence is the feature when privacy is the point, and the cost when it is not.

faq: Not from the stripped file. Order survives (points keep their sequence), so relative pacing is implicit in spacing — but absolute time is gone by design.
Does point order still show the direction?
Yes — sequence remains, so start-to-finish direction reads as before. Reversing is a different tool's job, and an untimed file reverses just as well.
Some training platforms require times for activity imports and may refuse or assume. Route-oriented platforms accept timeless geometry happily — know your destination's appetite.
A timeless file cannot testify about pace — which protects privacy and forfeits proof in equal measure. Keep originals for anything contested.
This tool strips the whole file. Split first (per-day files), strip the public day, keep the rest timed.
Does it also remove the file's own created date?
Yes — metadata <time> goes too, as the table states. A stripped file that confesses its birthday in the header would be theatre, not privacy.
